items.title: How Large Language Models Work (Without the Maths)
items.excerpt: A clear explanation of large language models: tokens, next-word prediction, training, context windows, temperature, why they hallucinate, and how to use them well.
items.content:
Short answer: a large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on enormous amounts of text to do one thing: predict the next piece of text. Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, lets it write answers, code, summaries and conversations.

That sounds too simple to explain what chat assistants can do. This guide shows how such a simple goal leads to such capable behaviour, and why the same mechanism explains their mistakes.

Step 1: Text becomes tokens

Models don't read letters or whole words. Text is split into tokens: common words, parts of words, punctuation and spaces.

"Learning Python is fun!"  →  ["Learning", " Python", " is", " fun", "!"]
"unbelievably"             →  ["un", "believ", "ably"]

Each token is mapped to a number, and each number to a list of values (a vector) that captures something about its meaning. Words used in similar ways end up with similar vectors: "cat" is closer to "dog" than to "carburettor".

Why it matters to you: usage limits, prices and the model's memory are all measured in tokens. In English, a token averages roughly three-quarters of a word; other languages and code often use more tokens for the same content.

Step 2: Predict the next token

Given some text, the model calculates a probability for every possible next token:

Input:  "The capital of France is"
Output: " Paris" 92%   " a" 3%   " located" 2%   ...

It picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats:

"The capital of France is" → " Paris" → "." → " It" → " is" → " known" → ...

That's the whole generation process: one token at a time, each chosen based on everything before it. A long answer is thousands of these predictions in a row.

Step 3: How it learned to predict so well

Pre-training

The model starts with random parameters (billions of adjustable numbers) and reads a huge collection of text: books, websites, code, articles. For each position, it guesses the next token, checks the real one, and adjusts its parameters slightly to make the right answer more likely. Repeated trillions of times, this forces the model to absorb grammar, facts, writing styles, programming patterns and a great deal of reasoning-like structure, because all of those help predict text.

To predict the next line of a Python function, it helps to "know" Python. To predict the end of a maths explanation, it helps to follow the steps. Capability emerges from prediction.

The transformer and attention

Most LLMs use an architecture called the transformer. Its key idea is attention: when processing each token, the model looks at all the other tokens in the text and decides which ones matter most. In "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big", attention helps link "it" to "trophy". Stacking many layers of attention lets the model connect ideas across long passages.

Fine-tuning and feedback

A pre-trained model is a powerful text predictor but not a helpful assistant: ask it a question and it might continue with more questions. So it's further trained on examples of good conversations, and refined with feedback from people (and other techniques) that reward helpful, accurate and safe answers. This step turns a predictor into an assistant.

The context window: the model's working memory

The model only "sees" the text currently in its context window: your messages, its replies, any documents you pasted, and instructions from the app. That's measured in tokens and is limited, though modern windows are large.

Practical consequences:

  • In a very long conversation, early details may fall out of the window or get less attention.
  • The model doesn't remember previous conversations unless the app stores and re-inserts them.
  • Giving the relevant information in the prompt is the most reliable way to get accurate answers about your specific situation.

Temperature: why answers vary

When choosing the next token, the model doesn't always pick the most likely one. A setting often called temperature controls randomness:

  • Low temperature: picks likely tokens; more predictable and focused. Good for code and facts.
  • High temperature: more varied choices; more creative, but more likely to go off track.

That's why asking the same question twice can give different answers.

Why LLMs "hallucinate"

An LLM generates plausible text. Usually plausible and true overlap, because it learned from lots of accurate writing. But when it lacks the information, it doesn't stop; it produces text that sounds right: a confident fake citation, an API function that doesn't exist, a wrong date.

Ways to reduce this:

  • Give it the source material and ask it to answer only from that.
  • Ask for sources or reasoning you can check.
  • Use tools: many assistants can search the web, run code or query databases, grounding answers in real data.
  • Verify anything important: run the code, check the docs, confirm the facts.

What LLMs are great at

  • Drafting, rewriting and summarising text.
  • Explaining concepts at different levels ("explain recursion to a 12-year-old").
  • Writing and explaining code, generating tests, finding likely bugs.
  • Transforming formats: notes to email, JSON to a table, English to Hindi.
  • Brainstorming options and asking you good questions.

Where to be careful

  • Exact facts, numbers, legal or medical advice: check them.
  • Maths and long precise procedures: ask it to use a code or calculation tool, or check the result.
  • Recent events: the model's knowledge stops at its training date unless connected to live sources.
  • Private data: follow your organisation's rules about what you paste into AI tools.

How developers use LLMs in apps

Applications call LLMs through an API: send a prompt (and settings), get text back. Common patterns:

  • Prompting with instructions: a "system" message that defines the assistant's role and rules.
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): search your own documents for relevant passages, put them in the prompt, and ask the model to answer from them. This is how "chat with your docs" tools work.
  • Tool use / function calling: the model decides to call functions you provide (search, calculator, database), and you return the results to it.
  • Agents: a model that plans and takes several steps with tools to complete a task. See What Are AI Agents?.

If you know Python, calling an LLM API is a few lines of code, which makes the Python course a great starting point.

Frequently asked questions

Does the model search the internet for every answer?

Not by itself. The base model answers from patterns learned in training. Some apps add a search tool and pass the results to the model.

Does an LLM understand what it says?

It builds rich internal representations of language and concepts, which is why it can be so useful, but it doesn't have beliefs or experiences like a person. Treat it as a very capable pattern-based tool, not an authority.

Why does it sometimes get simple things wrong, like counting letters?

Tokens: the model sees "strawberry" as a few chunks, not individual letters, so letter-level tasks are surprisingly hard for it. Asking it to write and run code for such tasks works far better.

Is bigger always better?

Larger models are generally more capable, but smaller ones are faster and cheaper, and are often good enough for focused tasks. Many products use a mix.

Summary

  • LLMs split text into tokens and predict the next token, one at a time.
  • They learn by predicting text across enormous datasets, then are fine-tuned to be helpful.
  • The context window is their working memory; temperature controls randomness.
  • They can hallucinate because they generate plausible text; give them sources and verify important output.
  • Developers use them through APIs with patterns like RAG, tool use and agents.

items.title: CSS Grid Layouts
items.excerpt: Build full page layouts with grid-template-areas, make responsive card grids with auto-fit and minmax(), and combine Grid with Flexbox.
items.content:
With the basics of Grid in place, you can build complete page layouts. Two features make Grid especially powerful: named areas, which let you draw your layout in the CSS, and auto-fit with minmax(), which makes grids responsive without a single media query.

Named grid areas

grid-template-areas lets you name regions of the grid and arrange them like a map:

<style>
  .page {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
    grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header  header"
      "sidebar main"
      "footer  footer";
    gap: 10px;
    min-height: 360px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .page > * { padding: 16px; border-radius: 8px; }
  .page header { grid-area: header; background: #1e293b; color: white; }
  .page aside  { grid-area: sidebar; background: #e2e8f0; }
  .page main   { grid-area: main; background: #f8fafc; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; }
  .page footer { grid-area: footer; background: #cbd5e1; }
</style>
<div class="page">
  <header>Header</header>
  <aside>Sidebar</aside>
  <main>Main content</main>
  <footer>Footer</footer>
</div>
  • Each string in grid-template-areas is one row; each word is one cell.
  • Repeating a name (header header) makes that area span those cells.
  • Each item is assigned with grid-area: name.
  • A . means an empty cell.

The CSS now looks like a picture of the layout, which makes it easy to read and change.

Rearranging for phones

The real magic: to change the layout on small screens, you only redraw the map. You'll learn media queries properly in the next lesson; here's a preview:

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header"
      "main"
      "sidebar"
      "footer";
  }
}

On phones, everything stacks in one column, and the sidebar moves below the main content. The HTML doesn't change.

Responsive cards with auto-fit and minmax()

This one line creates a card grid that adapts to any screen width:

<style>
  .cards {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr));
    gap: 14px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .cards article {
    border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;
    border-radius: 10px;
    padding: 16px;
    background: white;
  }
</style>
<div class="cards">
  <article><h3>HTML</h3><p>Structure</p></article>
  <article><h3>CSS</h3><p>Style</p></article>
  <article><h3>JavaScript</h3><p>Behaviour</p></article>
  <article><h3>SQL</h3><p>Data</p></article>
  <article><h3>Python</h3><p>Everything else</p></article>
</div>

Resize the result pane and the number of columns changes by itself. Here's how it works:

  • minmax(180px, 1fr): each column is at least 180px, and at most one equal share of the space.
  • repeat(auto-fit, …): create as many columns as fit.

On a phone you get one column; on a laptop, four or five. No media queries needed.

auto-fit vs auto-fill

  • auto-fit stretches the existing items to fill the row when there are only a few.
  • auto-fill keeps empty "ghost" columns, so a few items stay at their minimum width.

For card grids, auto-fit is usually what you want.

A blog layout

<style>
  .blog {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 260px;
    gap: 24px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .posts {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr));
    gap: 16px;
  }
  .post { border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 10px; overflow: hidden; }
  .post img { width: 100%; height: 110px; object-fit: cover; display: block; }
  .post h3 { font-size: 16px; margin: 10px 12px 14px; }
  .side { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 16px; border-radius: 10px; align-self: start; }
</style>
<div class="blog">
  <div class="posts">
    <article class="post"><img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1/400/220" alt="" width="400" height="220"><h3>Getting started with Git</h3></article>
    <article class="post"><img src="https://picsum.photos/id/2/400/220" alt="" width="400" height="220"><h3>10 VS Code shortcuts</h3></article>
    <article class="post"><img src="https://picsum.photos/id/3/400/220" alt="" width="400" height="220"><h3>What is an API?</h3></article>
  </div>
  <aside class="side"><h3>Popular</h3><p>CSS Flexbox Basics</p><p>Python Lists</p></aside>
</div>

The outer grid makes two columns: posts and sidebar. The inner grid is a responsive card grid. minmax(0, 1fr) stops long content from stretching the column. align-self: start keeps the sidebar from stretching to the full height.

Grid and Flexbox together

A good rule of thumb:

  • Grid for the overall layout (the page, the card grid).
  • Flexbox inside components (the content of each card, a header's nav links, a button with an icon).

You don't have to choose one. Most modern sites use both, often on the same page.

Common mistakes

  • Area names that don't form rectangles. Each named area must be a rectangle; L-shapes aren't allowed.
  • Different numbers of cells in each row of grid-template-areas.
  • **Forgetting grid-area** on the items, so they ignore the map.
  • Columns that overflow because of long words or wide images: use minmax(0, 1fr) and max-width: 100% on images.

Exercise

  1. Build the header / sidebar / main / footer layout with named areas.
  2. Add the media query so it stacks on narrow screens, with the sidebar under the main content.
  3. Create a responsive grid of 8 cards with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)).
  4. Inside each card, use Flexbox to put an icon and a title side by side.

Summary

  • grid-template-areas draws the layout; grid-area places items.
  • Redraw the areas in a media query to rearrange the layout for phones.
  • repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min, 1fr)) creates responsive grids without media queries.
  • Use Grid for layout and Flexbox for components.

Next, you'll make every page work on phones, tablets and desktops with responsive design and media queries.
items.subject: css

items.title: CSS Responsive Design and Media Queries
items.excerpt: Make pages work on every screen: the viewport meta tag, mobile-first CSS, media queries and breakpoints, fluid type with clamp(), and testing on real sizes.
items.content:
Most people visit websites on their phones. Responsive design means one page that adapts its layout to any screen, from a small phone to a wide monitor. In this lesson you'll learn the tools: the viewport tag, flexible sizes, media queries and fluid typography.

Step 1: the viewport meta tag

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

Without this line in the <head>, phones pretend to be a 980px-wide desktop and shrink the whole page down to tiny, unreadable text. With it, the page uses the phone's real width. Every responsive page needs it.

Step 2: flexible foundations

Much of responsive design is just avoiding fixed sizes. You've already learned the basics:

  • max-width instead of width for containers.
  • max-width: 100%; height: auto; for images.
  • fr, % and flex for columns.
  • rem for text and spacing.
  • repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)) for card grids.

Get these right and a page is already 80% responsive before you write a single media query.

Media queries

A media query applies CSS only when a condition is true, usually a minimum or maximum screen width:

<style>
  .banner {
    padding: 16px;
    background: #fde68a;
    font: 18px system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  @media (min-width: 600px) {
    .banner { background: #a7f3d0; }
    .banner::after { content: " (600px or wider)"; }
  }
  @media (min-width: 900px) {
    .banner { background: #bfdbfe; }
    .banner::after { content: " (900px or wider)"; }
  }
</style>
<div class="banner">Resize the result pane</div>

The rules inside @media (min-width: 600px) { … } only apply when the window is at least 600px wide.

Mobile-first

There are two ways to write media queries:

  • Desktop-first: write the desktop layout, then use max-width queries to fix it for smaller screens.
  • Mobile-first: write the simple phone layout first (with no media query), then use min-width queries to add columns as space grows.

Mobile-first is the recommended approach: phone layouts are usually simpler (one column), so you start simple and add complexity, instead of undoing it.

<style>
  .layout { display: grid; gap: 12px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .layout > div { background: #e0e7ff; padding: 16px; border-radius: 8px; }

  /* Tablets: two columns */
  @media (min-width: 600px) {
    .layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
  }

  /* Desktops: sidebar + main + sidebar */
  @media (min-width: 900px) {
    .layout { grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 200px; }
  }
</style>
<div class="layout">
  <div>Menu</div>
  <div>Main content</div>
  <div>Related links</div>
</div>

Choosing breakpoints

A breakpoint is a width where the layout changes. Don't design for particular phone models; there are thousands. Instead, widen the browser slowly and add a breakpoint where the design starts to look wrong. Common starting points:

Two or three breakpoints are enough for most sites.

A responsive navigation

<style>
  .nav { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; background: #1e293b; padding: 12px; }
  .nav ul { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 4px; }
  .nav a { color: white; text-decoration: none; display: block; padding: 8px; }

  @media (min-width: 600px) {
    .nav ul { flex-direction: row; gap: 16px; }
  }
</style>
<nav class="nav">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="#">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="#">Tutorials</a></li>
    <li><a href="#">Blog</a></li>
    <li><a href="#">Contact</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

Stacked on phones, in a row on larger screens. (A real site often hides the menu behind a "☰" button on phones; that needs a little JavaScript, which you'll learn in the JavaScript course.)

Fluid typography with clamp()

Headings that look great on a desktop are often too big on a phone. clamp() scales text smoothly between a minimum and maximum:

h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 4vw + 1rem, 3rem);
}

clamp(min, preferred, max): the heading is never smaller than 1.75rem, never larger than 3rem, and scales with the window width in between. No breakpoints needed.

Other useful media features

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  body { background: #0f172a; color: #e2e8f0; }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; }
}

@media (hover: hover) {
  .card:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }
}

@media print {
  nav, footer, .ads { display: none; }
}
  • prefers-color-scheme: the user's light or dark mode setting.
  • prefers-reduced-motion: the user asked for less animation (some people get dizzy).
  • hover: whether the device can hover (phones can't).
  • print: styles for printing.

Testing responsive pages

  • Browser device mode: press F12, then the phone/tablet icon (Ctrl + Shift + M). Choose sizes or drag the width.
  • Test on a real phone, too: touch targets, font sizes and fixed elements feel different in your hand.
  • Check that there's no horizontal scrolling at 320px wide, the narrowest common phone width.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the viewport meta tag.
  • Fixed widths like width: 960px on containers.
  • Too many breakpoints for specific devices.
  • Tiny tap targets. Buttons and links should be at least about 44 × 44 pixels on touch screens.
  • Hiding important content on mobile. Phone users need the same information.

Exercise

  1. Take your profile page and make it mobile-first: one column by default.
  2. At 700px, show the skills and projects sections side by side.
  3. Make the main heading fluid with clamp().
  4. Add a prefers-color-scheme: dark block with dark colours.
  5. Test it at 320px, 768px and 1280px widths in device mode.

Summary

  • Always include the viewport meta tag.
  • Flexible units and layouts do most of the work; media queries handle the rest.
  • Write mobile-first CSS and add min-width breakpoints where the design needs them.
  • clamp() makes text fluid; media features handle dark mode, motion, hover and print.

Next, you'll add smooth movement with CSS transitions.
items.subject: css

items.title: CSS Transitions and Transforms
items.excerpt: Animate changes smoothly with transition, move, scale and rotate elements with transform, choose easing, and add simple keyframe animations responsibly.
items.content:
When a button changes colour on hover, the change normally happens instantly. A transition makes it happen smoothly over a short time. Combined with transforms (move, scale, rotate), transitions give a site a polished, responsive feel with very little code.

A first transition

<style>
  .btn {
    background: #2563eb;
    color: white;
    border: none;
    padding: 12px 24px;
    border-radius: 8px;
    font-size: 16px;
    transition: background-color 0.3s ease;
  }
  .btn:hover {
    background-color: #1e3a8a;
  }
</style>
<button class="btn">Hover over me</button>

The transition goes on the normal state, not the hover state, so the change animates both when the mouse arrives and when it leaves.

The parts of a transition

transition: property duration timing-function delay;
  • property: what to animate (background-color, transform, opacity), or all.
  • duration: how long, e.g. 0.2s or 200ms.
  • timing function: the speed curve.
  • delay (optional): wait before starting.

Several properties can be listed with commas:

.card {
  transition: transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease;
}

Avoid transition: all: it can animate things you didn't intend and is slower.

Timing functions

<style>
  .track { background: #f1f5f9; margin-bottom: 6px; padding: 4px; font: 13px system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .ball {
    width: 90px; padding: 6px; background: #8b5cf6; color: white; border-radius: 999px; text-align: center;
    transition: transform 1.2s;
  }
  .tracks:hover .ball { transform: translateX(220px); }
</style>
<div class="tracks">
  <p>Hover over this area:</p>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: linear;">linear</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease;">ease</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease-in;">ease-in</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease-out;">ease-out</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease-in-out;">ease-in-out</div></div>
</div>
  • ease (default): starts fast, ends slow. Good general choice.
  • ease-out: fast start, gentle stop. Great for things appearing.
  • ease-in: slow start. Good for things leaving.
  • linear: constant speed. Mostly for spinners.
  • cubic-bezier(...) creates custom curves.

Transforms

transform changes how an element is drawn without affecting the layout around it:

transform: translateX(20px);       /* move right */
transform: translateY(-4px);       /* move up */
transform: scale(1.05);            /* 5% bigger */
transform: rotate(45deg);          /* rotate */
transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02);  /* combine several */

Because transforms don't move other elements, they're smooth and cheap for the browser to animate.

A lifting card

<style>
  body { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 30px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .card {
    width: 240px;
    background: white;
    padding: 20px;
    border-radius: 12px;
    box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1);
    transition: transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease;
  }
  .card:hover {
    transform: translateY(-6px);
    box-shadow: 0 12px 24px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15);
  }
</style>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Hover me</h3>
  <p>I lift up and my shadow grows.</p>
</div>

Which properties to animate

For smooth, 60-frames-per-second animation, prefer **transform and opacity**. Animating width, height, top, left or margin forces the browser to recalculate the layout on every frame, which can stutter on phones.

Keyframe animations

Transitions animate between two states. Animations can run on their own, loop, and have many steps:

<style>
  @keyframes pulse {
    0%   { transform: scale(1); }
    50%  { transform: scale(1.08); }
    100% { transform: scale(1); }
  }
  @keyframes spin {
    to { transform: rotate(360deg); }
  }
  .live { display: inline-block; background: #ef4444; color: white; padding: 6px 14px; border-radius: 999px; animation: pulse 1.5s ease-in-out infinite; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .spinner { width: 32px; height: 32px; border: 4px solid #e2e8f0; border-top-color: #2563eb; border-radius: 50%; animation: spin 0.8s linear infinite; margin-top: 16px; }
</style>
<span class="live">● LIVE</span>
<div class="spinner" role="status" aria-label="Loading"></div>
  • @keyframes name { ... } defines the steps.
  • animation: name duration timing-function iteration-count; runs it.
  • infinite loops forever.

Respect reduced motion

Some people get dizzy or sick from movement on screen and turn on "reduce motion" in their system settings. Honour it:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

Good practice

  • Keep UI transitions short: 150–300ms. Longer feels slow.
  • Animate to give feedback (hover, open, close), not just for decoration.
  • Avoid things that flash more than three times a second.

Common mistakes

  • **Putting transition only on :hover**, so the change animates in but snaps back out.
  • Animating layout properties like width and top instead of transform.
  • **transition: all** catching unintended changes.
  • Endless decorative animations that distract from the content.

Exercise

  1. Give your buttons a 200ms colour transition on hover.
  2. Make cards lift with translateY and a bigger shadow on hover.
  3. Create a loading spinner with @keyframes.
  4. Add the reduced-motion media query to your stylesheet.

Summary

  • transition: property duration timing animates changes between states.
  • transform moves, scales and rotates without affecting layout.
  • Animate transform and opacity for smooth results.
  • @keyframes creates standalone animations; always respect prefers-reduced-motion.

Next, you'll learn CSS variables, which make large stylesheets easy to manage and theme.
items.subject: css

items.title: CSS Variables
items.excerpt: Store colours, spacing and fonts in custom properties, use var() with fallbacks, build a dark mode, and organise a stylesheet around design tokens.
items.content:
In a real stylesheet, the same brand colour may appear fifty times. Changing it means fifty edits. CSS variables (officially "custom properties") let you store a value once and reuse it everywhere. They also make dark mode and themes easy.

Defining and using a variable

<style>
  :root {
    --brand: #2563eb;
    --radius: 10px;
  }
  .btn {
    background: var(--brand);
    color: white;
    border: none;
    padding: 10px 20px;
    border-radius: var(--radius);
  }
  .link { color: var(--brand); }
  .box { border: 2px solid var(--brand); border-radius: var(--radius); padding: 12px; margin-top: 12px; }
</style>
<button class="btn">Button</button>
<a class="link" href="#">A link</a>
<div class="box">A box</div>
  • A variable name starts with two hyphens: --brand.
  • :root means the <html> element, so variables defined there are available everywhere.
  • var(--brand) uses the value.

Now change --brand to #16a34a and everything turns green at once.

Fallback values

.title { color: var(--heading-color, #111827); }

If --heading-color isn't defined, the fallback after the comma is used.

Variables are inherited and can be overridden

A variable can be redefined on any element, and the new value applies to that element and its children:

<style>
  :root { --accent: #2563eb; }
  .card { border-top: 4px solid var(--accent); padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 10px; background: #f8fafc; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .card h3 { color: var(--accent); margin: 0; }
  .card.success { --accent: #16a34a; }
  .card.danger  { --accent: #dc2626; }
</style>
<div class="card"><h3>Default</h3></div>
<div class="card success"><h3>Success</h3></div>
<div class="card danger"><h3>Danger</h3></div>

One set of card styles, three colour variants, each changing just one variable. This is how design systems build components.

A dark mode in a few lines

<style>
  :root {
    --bg: #ffffff;
    --text: #1f2937;
    --muted: #6b7280;
    --surface: #f3f4f6;
    --brand: #2563eb;
  }
  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
    :root {
      --bg: #0f172a;
      --text: #e5e7eb;
      --muted: #94a3b8;
      --surface: #1e293b;
      --brand: #60a5fa;
    }
  }
  body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; padding: 20px; }
  .panel { background: var(--surface); padding: 16px; border-radius: 10px; }
  .panel p { color: var(--muted); }
  a { color: var(--brand); }
</style>
<div class="panel">
  <h3>Automatic dark mode</h3>
  <p>Switch your system to dark mode and this page follows.</p>
  <a href="#">A link</a>
</div>

The components only use variables. Dark mode simply swaps the variable values. VitalStack's own dark mode works this way, with a toggle button that sets a data-theme attribute on <html>:

:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg: #0f172a;
  --text: #e5e7eb;
}

Design tokens: organising variables

Large projects group their variables by purpose. These are often called design tokens:

:root {
  /* Colours */
  --color-brand: #2563eb;
  --color-text: #1f2937;
  --color-muted: #6b7280;
  --color-border: #e5e7eb;

  /* Spacing scale */
  --space-1: 0.25rem;
  --space-2: 0.5rem;
  --space-3: 1rem;
  --space-4: 1.5rem;
  --space-5: 2rem;

  /* Typography */
  --font-body: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif;
  --font-code: "Source Code Pro", monospace;
  --text-sm: 0.875rem;
  --text-lg: 1.25rem;

  /* Shapes */
  --radius-sm: 6px;
  --radius-lg: 14px;
  --shadow: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.08);
}

Using a fixed scale (--space-3 instead of random values like 13px, 17px, 22px) makes a design look consistent.

Calculating with variables

:root { --gap: 16px; }
.section { padding: calc(var(--gap) * 2); }
.tight { margin-top: calc(var(--gap) / 2); }

calc() combines variables with maths, even mixing units: calc(100% - var(--sidebar-width)).

Changing variables with JavaScript

<style>
  :root { --hue: 220; }
  .swatch { height: 80px; border-radius: 8px; background: hsl(var(--hue) 80% 55%); }
</style>
<div class="swatch"></div>
<label>Hue <input type="range" min="0" max="360" value="220" id="hue"></label>
<script>
  document.getElementById("hue").addEventListener("input", function () {
    document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--hue", this.value);
  });
</script>

Drag the slider and the colour updates live. Variables are the bridge between JavaScript and CSS.

Common mistakes

  • One hyphen instead of two: -brand isn't a variable.
  • **Forgetting var()**: color: --brand; does nothing.
  • Spaces or typos in names; variable names are case-sensitive.
  • Defining variables inside one component and expecting them to work in others. Put shared ones in :root.

Exercise

  1. Move your profile page's colours, radius and spacing into :root variables.
  2. Add a dark mode with prefers-color-scheme by redefining only the variables.
  3. Make "success", "warning" and "danger" versions of a message box by changing one variable each.
  4. Add a range slider that changes a variable with JavaScript.

Summary

  • Define variables with --name: value (usually on :root) and use them with var(--name).
  • Variables inherit and can be overridden per element, which makes component variants easy.
  • Dark mode = swap variable values.
  • Design tokens (colours, spacing, fonts) keep a whole site consistent.

Next, you'll use the whole CSS course to style your profile page project.
items.subject: css

items.title: CSS Project: Style Your Profile Page
items.excerpt: Turn the plain HTML profile page into a modern, responsive design with variables, Flexbox, Grid, cards, a dark mode and smooth transitions.
items.content:
At the end of the HTML course you built a complete profile page. Now you'll make it look professional using everything from this course: variables, the box model, Flexbox, Grid, responsive design and transitions. Work through the steps in order, testing as you go.

Step 0: Start with your HTML

Use your page from the HTML project. If you don't have it, this short version is enough to follow along:

<header class="site-header">
  <div class="container header-inner">
    <a class="logo" href="#">Asha Verma</a>
    <nav aria-label="Main">
      <ul class="nav">
        <li><a href="#about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="#skills">Skills</a></li>
        <li><a href="#projects">Projects</a></li>
        <li><a href="#contact">Contact</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </div>
</header>
<main class="container">
  <section id="about" class="hero">
    <img class="avatar" src="https://picsum.photos/id/64/240/240" alt="Asha smiling at a desk" width="240" height="240">
    <div>
      <h1>Hi, I'm Asha</h1>
      <p class="lead">Beginner web developer building one small project every week.</p>
      <a class="btn" href="#contact">Get in touch</a>
    </div>
  </section>
  <section id="projects">
    <h2>Projects</h2>
    <div class="cards">
      <article class="card"><h3>Recipe page</h3><p>Headings, lists and images.</p></article>
      <article class="card"><h3>Timetable</h3><p>Tables with merged cells.</p></article>
      <article class="card"><h3>Profile page</h3><p>Everything together, now with CSS.</p></article>
    </div>
  </section>
</main>
<footer class="site-footer"><div class="container"><small>© Asha Verma</small></div></footer>

The only change from plain HTML: a few classes added as styling hooks.

Step 1: Variables and a reset

Put this at the top of your stylesheet (or a <style> element while testing):

:root {
  --bg: #f8fafc;
  --surface: #ffffff;
  --text: #1f2937;
  --muted: #64748b;
  --border: #e2e8f0;
  --brand: #2563eb;
  --brand-dark: #1e40af;
  --radius: 14px;
  --shadow: 0 4px 14px rgb(15 23 42 / 0.08);
  --font: "Inter", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif;
}

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

body {
  margin: 0;
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
  font-family: var(--font);
  line-height: 1.6;
}

img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }

Step 2: A centred container

.container {
  max-width: 1000px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 0 20px;
}

Every section now lines up on the same centred column.

Step 3: Header with Flexbox

.site-header {
  background: var(--surface);
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border);
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  z-index: 10;
}
.header-inner {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 12px;
  padding-block: 14px;
}
.logo {
  font-weight: 800;
  font-size: 1.25rem;
  color: var(--text);
  text-decoration: none;
}
.nav {
  display: flex;
  gap: 4px;
  list-style: none;
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
}
.nav a {
  display: block;
  padding: 8px 12px;
  border-radius: 8px;
  color: var(--muted);
  text-decoration: none;
  transition: background-color 0.2s, color 0.2s;
}
.nav a:hover {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--brand);
}

(padding-block sets top and bottom padding together.)

Step 4: The hero section

.hero {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  align-items: center;
  text-align: center;
  gap: 24px;
  padding: 48px 0;
}
.avatar {
  width: 160px;
  height: 160px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  object-fit: cover;
  border: 4px solid var(--surface);
  box-shadow: var(--shadow);
}
.hero h1 {
  font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.15;
  margin: 0 0 8px;
}
.lead {
  font-size: 1.15rem;
  color: var(--muted);
  max-width: 45ch;
  margin: 0 auto 20px;
}
@media (min-width: 700px) {
  .hero {
    flex-direction: row;
    text-align: left;
  }
  .lead { margin-left: 0; }
}

Mobile-first: stacked and centred on phones, photo beside text from 700px.

Step 5: Buttons

.btn {
  display: inline-block;
  background: var(--brand);
  color: white;
  padding: 12px 24px;
  border-radius: 999px;
  font-weight: 600;
  text-decoration: none;
  transition: background-color 0.2s, transform 0.2s;
}
.btn:hover {
  background: var(--brand-dark);
  transform: translateY(-2px);
}
.btn:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #f59e0b;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

Step 6: Responsive project cards with Grid

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 20px;
}
.card {
  background: var(--surface);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  padding: 20px;
  box-shadow: var(--shadow);
  transition: transform 0.2s, box-shadow 0.2s;
}
.card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px);
  box-shadow: 0 12px 24px rgb(15 23 42 / 0.12);
}
.card h3 { margin-top: 0; }
.card p { color: var(--muted); margin-bottom: 0; }

Step 7: Footer, forms and tables

.site-footer {
  margin-top: 64px;
  padding: 24px 0;
  border-top: 1px solid var(--border);
  color: var(--muted);
  text-align: center;
}

input, textarea {
  width: 100%;
  padding: 10px 12px;
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: 8px;
  font: inherit;
  background: var(--surface);
  color: var(--text);
}
input:focus, textarea:focus {
  outline: none;
  border-color: var(--brand);
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px rgb(37 99 235 / 0.25);
}

table { width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; }
th, td { padding: 10px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border); text-align: left; }
tbody tr:nth-child(even) { background: var(--bg); }

font: inherit makes form fields use the page font instead of the browser's default. border-collapse: collapse merges table borders into single lines. The focus style replaces the outline with an equally visible ring, so keyboard users can still see where they are.

Step 8: Dark mode

Because everything uses variables, dark mode is one block:

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --bg: #0b1120;
    --surface: #111827;
    --text: #e5e7eb;
    --muted: #94a3b8;
    --border: #1f2937;
    --brand: #60a5fa;
    --brand-dark: #3b82f6;
  }
}

Step 9: Final checks

  • ☐ Test at 320px, 768px and 1280px wide: no horizontal scrolling.
  • ☐ Tab through the page: every link and button shows focus.
  • ☐ Check text contrast in both light and dark mode.
  • ☐ Turn on "reduce motion" and add the reduced-motion block from the transitions lesson.
  • ☐ Validate the CSS at jigsaw.w3.org/css-validator.

Ideas to go further

  • Add a skills section as a row of pill-shaped tags with flex-wrap.
  • Add a theme toggle button (you'll be able to write the JavaScript after the first few JavaScript lessons).
  • Publish it for free on GitHub Pages or Netlify and share the link.

Summary

  • Variables and a small reset give a consistent foundation.
  • Flexbox handles the header and hero; Grid handles the card layout.
  • Mobile-first media queries and clamp() make it responsive.
  • Variables make dark mode a single block of CSS.

You've finished the CSS course. Next comes JavaScript, where you'll make your pages interactive.
items.subject: css

items.title: JavaScript Introduction
items.excerpt: What JavaScript is, what it can do in the browser and beyond, how it relates to HTML and CSS, and your first lines of code.
items.content:
HTML gives a page structure and CSS makes it look good. JavaScript makes it do things: respond to clicks, check forms, load new data without reloading, show and hide menus, run games. It's the only programming language that runs natively in every web browser, which makes it one of the most useful languages you can learn.

Your first JavaScript

console.log("Hello, world!");
console.log(2 + 3);

Click Try it Yourself and press Run. You'll see Hello, world! and 5 in the output. console.log() prints a value to the console, a panel developers use to see what their code is doing. You'll use it in almost every lesson.

JavaScript changes the page

Here's JavaScript working with HTML:

<h2 id="greeting">Hello!</h2>
<button id="btn">Click me</button>

<script>
  const button = document.getElementById("btn");
  const heading = document.getElementById("greeting");

  button.addEventListener("click", function () {
    heading.textContent = "You clicked the button!";
  });
</script>

Click the button and the heading changes. In three steps, the script:

  1. Finds the button and the heading on the page.
  2. Waits for a click on the button.
  3. Changes the heading's text when the click happens.

Almost every interactive feature on the web follows this pattern: find elements, listen for something, change something.

HTML, CSS and JavaScript together

What JavaScript can do

In the browser:

  • React to clicks, typing, scrolling and other events.
  • Change any HTML or CSS on the page.
  • Check form input before it's sent.
  • Load data from servers (weather, search results, new posts) without reloading.
  • Save small amounts of data in the browser, e.g. a dark-mode preference.
  • Draw graphics and run games.

Outside the browser, with Node.js, JavaScript also runs web servers, command-line tools and desktop apps. Learn it once and use it nearly everywhere.

JavaScript is not Java

Despite the name, JavaScript has nothing to do with Java. The name was a marketing decision in 1995. The official standard is called ECMAScript; "ES6" or "ES2015" refers to a big update that added modern features like let, const and arrow functions, which you'll learn in this course.

A taste of the language

let name = "Asha";
let age = 21;

if (age >= 18) {
  console.log(name + " is an adult.");
} else {
  console.log(name + " is a minor.");
}

for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  console.log("Counting: " + i);
}

Don't worry about understanding every line yet. You'll learn variables, if statements and loops step by step. Notice that it reads almost like English.

Statements and semicolons

A JavaScript program is a list of statements, instructions run from top to bottom. Each one usually ends with a semicolon ;. JavaScript can often add missing semicolons automatically, but writing them yourself avoids rare, confusing bugs. This course always uses them.

Comments

// A single-line comment

/*
  A comment that
  spans several lines
*/

console.log("Comments are ignored when the code runs.");

Case sensitivity

JavaScript is case-sensitive: name, Name and NAME are three different things, and console.Log() (capital L) is an error. When something doesn't work, check the capitalisation first.

How to practise

  • Use Try it Yourself on every example in this course and change things.
  • In any browser, press F12 (or Ctrl + Shift + J) and open the Console tab. You can type JavaScript there and press Enter to run it immediately.
  • Make mistakes on purpose and read the error messages. Learning to read errors is half of programming.

Common mistakes

  • Wrong capitalisation: Console.log or getElementByID.
  • Missing quotes around text: console.log(Hello) looks for a variable called Hello.
  • Mismatched brackets ( ) and braces { }.
  • Smart quotes pasted from a word processor (“ ”) instead of plain quotes (" ").

Exercise

  1. Print your name and your favourite food with two console.log() lines.
  2. Print the result of 7 * 6.
  3. In the button example, change the new heading text to something of your own.
  4. Open your browser's console on any website and type 2 ** 10. What do you get?

Summary

  • JavaScript adds behaviour to web pages and also runs on servers with Node.js.
  • console.log() prints values so you can see what your code does.
  • Interactive features follow the pattern: find elements, listen for events, change the page.
  • JavaScript is case-sensitive, and statements end with semicolons.

Next, you'll learn where to put JavaScript in an HTML page.
items.subject: javascript

items.title: Where to Put JavaScript
items.excerpt: Add JavaScript with script elements and external .js files, understand why placement matters, and load scripts correctly with defer.
items.content:
Just like CSS, JavaScript can live inside the HTML page or in a separate file. Where and how you load it affects whether it works at all, and how fast your page appears.

Inline script element

The simplest way is a <script> element with code inside it:

<p id="msg">Waiting…</p>

<script>
  document.getElementById("msg").textContent = "JavaScript is running!";
</script>

The browser reads the page from top to bottom. When it reaches <script>, it stops, runs the code, and then continues.

Why order matters

A script can only find elements that the browser has already read. This fails:

<script>
  // The paragraph doesn't exist yet when this runs
  const p = document.getElementById("late");
  console.log(p); // null
</script>

<p id="late">I come after the script.</p>

getElementById returns null ("nothing"), and trying to change null causes an error. That's why scripts used to be placed at the end of the body, after all the HTML:

<body>
  <h1>My page</h1>
  <p id="intro">Hello</p>

  <script>
    document.getElementById("intro").textContent = "Found it!";
  </script>
</body>

External JavaScript files

On real websites, JavaScript goes in its own file, for example js/main.js:

// js/main.js
console.log("main.js loaded");

Link it with the src attribute:

<script src="js/main.js"></script>
  • A <script> with src must be empty; any code between the tags is ignored.
  • The closing </script> tag is required.

Benefits are the same as for external CSS: one file shared by every page, cached by the browser, and clean HTML.

defer: the modern best practice

Put the script in the <head> with the defer attribute:

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My page</title>
  <script src="js/main.js" defer></script>
</head>

defer tells the browser:

  1. Download the file in the background while reading the HTML (no pause).
  2. Run it only after the whole page has been read, so every element exists.
  3. Run several deferred scripts in the order they appear.

This gives you the best of both: the download starts early, and your code can safely find any element. Use defer for almost all your scripts.

async

<script src="https://example.com/analytics.js" async></script>

async also downloads in the background, but runs the script as soon as it arrives, possibly before the page is finished and in any order. It's for independent scripts that don't touch your page's elements, such as analytics or ads.

The DOMContentLoaded event

If you must use a script in the head without defer (for example, inline code), wait for the page to be ready:

<script>
  document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
    document.getElementById("box").textContent = "The page is ready.";
  });
</script>
<p id="box">Loading…</p>

The code inside runs once the whole HTML has been read.

JavaScript modules

Modern code is often split into modules that import from each other:

<script type="module" src="js/app.js"></script>

Module scripts are deferred automatically and can use import and export. You'll meet them later; for now, defer is all you need.

Inline event attributes (avoid)

Old tutorials often show this:

<button onclick="alert('Hi!')">Old style</button>

It works, but mixing code into HTML is hard to maintain and blocked by strict security settings. Use addEventListener in your script instead, as you'll learn in the Events lesson.

Common mistakes

  • Script before the elements it uses, without defer: null errors.
  • **Code inside a <script src="…">**, which is silently ignored.
  • Wrong file path in src. Check the console and Network tab (F12) for a 404 error.
  • **Forgetting </script>**: <script src="x.js" /> is not valid.

Exercise

  1. Make a page with a paragraph and an inline script at the end of the body that changes its text.
  2. Move the script into main.js, link it in the head without defer, and see the error in the console.
  3. Add defer and check that it works again.
  4. Add console.log("one") in one deferred file and console.log("two") in a second; confirm the order.

Summary

  • JavaScript goes in <script> elements or external .js files linked with src.
  • Scripts can only find elements the browser has already read.
  • Use <script src="…" defer> in the head: it downloads early and runs when the page is ready.
  • Use async only for independent scripts like analytics.

Next, you'll learn the different ways to show output from JavaScript.

items.title: How the Web Works: What Happens When You Type a URL
items.excerpt: Follow a web request step by step: URLs, DNS, IP addresses, TCP and HTTPS, HTTP requests and responses, servers, and how the browser turns HTML, CSS and JavaScript into a page.
items.content:
Short answer: when you type a URL, your browser finds the server's address with DNS, opens a secure connection (TCP + TLS/HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, receives an HTTP response with HTML, then downloads the CSS, JavaScript and images it references, and finally renders the page. All of this usually happens in well under a second.

Understanding this journey makes you a better developer: it explains slow pages, broken sites, security warnings and how frontend and backend fit together.

Step 1: The URL

https://vitalstack.co.in/tutorials/html-introduction/?ref=home#examples
└─┬──┘   └──────┬───────┘└──────────┬────────────────┘└───┬───┘└───┬───┘
scheme       domain               path                  query   fragment
  • Scheme: https means use HTTP over a secure connection.
  • Domain: the human-friendly name of the server.
  • Path: which page or resource on that server.
  • Query string: extra parameters, often for searches and filters.
  • Fragment: a section within the page (#examples); never sent to the server, the browser just scrolls to it.

Step 2: DNS finds the server's address

Computers on the internet find each other by IP addresses like 203.0.113.42 (IPv4) or 2001:db8::42 (IPv6). Names like vitalstack.co.in are for humans.

DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone book:

  1. The browser checks its own cache: "Have I looked this up recently?"
  2. If not, it asks the operating system, which asks a DNS resolver (usually run by your internet provider, or a public one).
  3. The resolver asks the DNS hierarchy: the root servers point to the .in servers, which point to the servers responsible for co.in, which point to the domain's own DNS servers, which finally answer with the IP address.
  4. The answer is cached at each step for a while (its "TTL"), so the next lookup is instant.

This is why DNS changes (like moving a site to new hosting) can take time to "propagate": old answers stay cached until they expire.

Step 3: Connecting: TCP and TLS

The browser opens a TCP connection to the server's IP address on port 443 (the standard HTTPS port). TCP makes sure data arrives complete and in order.

Then comes the TLS handshake, which makes the connection secure:

  1. The server sends its certificate, proving it really is vitalstack.co.in (signed by a trusted certificate authority).
  2. The browser checks the certificate is valid, unexpired and for the right domain.
  3. Both sides agree on encryption keys.

Now everything sent is encrypted: nobody on the network (public Wi-Fi, your provider) can read or change it. That's the padlock in the address bar. If the certificate is wrong or expired, browsers show a security warning.

(Newer HTTP/3 connections use a protocol called QUIC instead of TCP, combining these steps to connect faster, but the ideas are the same.)

Step 4: The HTTP request

The browser sends a request: plain structured text (inside the encrypted connection):

GET /tutorials/html-introduction/?ref=home HTTP/1.1
Host: vitalstack.co.in
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (…)
Accept: text/html
Accept-Language: en-IN,en;q=0.9
Cookie: theme=dark
  • Method: GET (read a page). Others: POST (send data, like a form), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE.
  • Path of the resource.
  • Headers: extra information like the browser type, preferred languages, and cookies (small pieces of data the site stored earlier, e.g. that you're logged in).

Step 5: The server responds

On the server, a web server program (like Nginx, Apache or LiteSpeed) receives the request. Then:

  • For a static file (an image, a CSS file), it sends the file directly.
  • For a dynamic page, it runs application code (PHP for WordPress, Python, Node.js…), which might query a database, build the HTML, and return it.
  • Often a cache or CDN (content delivery network, servers spread around the world) answers instead, with a saved copy, which is much faster.

The response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Cache-Control: max-age=600
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>HTML Introduction</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
  <script src="/main.js" defer></script>
</head>
<body>…</body>
</html>
  • Status code: 200 OK. Others you'll see: 301/302 (redirect), 304 (not modified, use your cached copy), 404 (not found), 403 (forbidden), 500 (server error).
  • Headers: the content type, caching rules, cookies to store.
  • Body: the HTML itself.

Step 6: The browser renders the page

Now the browser turns text into pixels:

  1. Parse HTML into the DOM, a tree of elements (see our DOM lesson).
  2. Discover resources: the <link> to CSS, <script> tags, images and fonts. Each triggers another HTTP request (often over the same connection).
  3. Parse CSS into rules and match them to elements.
  4. Layout: calculate the size and position of every box (the CSS box model).
  5. Paint: draw text, colours, borders and images.
  6. Run JavaScript, which can change the DOM and trigger layout and paint again.

A typical page needs dozens of requests: HTML, stylesheets, scripts, fonts, images. That's why page speed depends on the number and size of resources, not just the HTML.

Why pages are slow (and how to fix it)

Browser developer tools (F12 → Network tab) show every request, its size and how long it took. Try it on any website.

Where frontend and backend fit

  • Frontend code runs in the browser: HTML, CSS and JavaScript from Step 6.
  • Backend code runs on the server in Step 5: application logic and databases.
  • They talk through HTTP. Modern apps often load a page once, then use JavaScript fetch() to exchange JSON with APIs without reloading (our fetch lesson).

See Frontend vs Backend vs Full-Stack for career paths on each side.

Frequently asked questions

What's the difference between the internet and the web?

The internet is the global network connecting computers. The web is one service that runs on it (pages and links over HTTP). Email and video calls also use the internet but aren't "the web".

Why does HTTPS matter if my site has no passwords?

It prevents others on the network from reading or modifying your pages (for example, injecting ads or malware), browsers warn users about non-HTTPS sites, and search engines prefer secure sites. Certificates are free from services like Let's Encrypt, and most hosting includes them.

What are cookies used for?

Remembering state between requests, since HTTP itself is "stateless": login sessions, preferences, shopping carts, and also analytics and advertising (which is why many sites ask for consent).

What is a CDN?

A network of servers around the world that keep copies of your site's files, so visitors download from a server near them. It makes sites faster and absorbs traffic spikes.

Summary

  • A URL has a scheme, domain, path, query and fragment.
  • DNS turns the domain into an IP address; TCP + TLS create a secure connection.
  • The browser sends an HTTP request; the server (or a cache/CDN) sends a response with a status code, headers and body.
  • The browser builds the DOM, loads CSS, JavaScript and images, lays out and paints the page.
  • Speed depends on the size and number of resources, server work and distance.

items.title: JavaScript Output (console.log)
items.excerpt: Show results with console.log and its relatives, write into the page with textContent, use alert sparingly, and debug with the browser console.
items.content:
A program is only useful if you can see what it's doing. JavaScript can show output in several places: the developer console, the web page itself, and pop-up dialogs. Each has its own job.

console.log(): your best friend

console.log("Hello");
console.log(42);
console.log(true);
console.log("Total:", 19.99, "INR");

console.log() prints to the browser's console. You can pass several values separated by commas, and they're printed with spaces between them.

Developers use it constantly to check what's happening: "What's in this variable right now?" "Did this part of the code even run?" It's invisible to normal visitors, so it doesn't affect the page.

Logging objects and arrays

const user = { name: "Asha", age: 21, skills: ["HTML", "CSS"] };
console.log(user);

const scores = [92, 87, 95];
console.log(scores);

The console shows the whole structure, which is very handy when working with data. In the browser's own console you can click to expand nested values.

Other console methods

console.info("Information");
console.warn("Careful: this looks wrong");
console.error("Something broke");

console.table([
  { language: "HTML", lessons: 20 },
  { language: "CSS", lessons: 20 },
  { language: "JavaScript", lessons: 25 }
]);
  • console.warn and console.error are shown in yellow and red in the browser console and are easy to filter.
  • console.table displays an array of objects as a neat table (open your browser's console with F12 to see it).

Template literals: easier messages

Joining text with + gets messy. Template literals use backticks (`) and ${ } to insert values:

const name = "Rohan";
const lessons = 7;

console.log("Hi " + name + ", you finished " + lessons + " lessons.");
console.log(`Hi ${name}, you finished ${lessons} lessons.`);
console.log(`Next lesson number: ${lessons + 1}`);

Both lines print the same thing, but the second is much easier to read and write. You can put any expression inside ${ }. You'll use template literals throughout the course.

Writing into the page

To show output to visitors, change an element's content:

<p id="result"></p>

<script>
  const price = 499;
  const qty = 3;
  document.getElementById("result").textContent = `Total: ₹${price * qty}`;
</script>

textContent sets the text inside an element. There's also innerHTML, which interprets the string as HTML:

<div id="box"></div>

<script>
  document.getElementById("box").innerHTML = "<strong>Bold</strong> and <em>italic</em>";
</script>

**Be careful with innerHTML:** never put text typed by users into it. If a user types <img src=x onerror=...>, the browser runs it as code, a security hole called cross-site scripting (XSS). Use textContent for plain text, which is always safe.

alert, confirm and prompt

<button id="a">Alert</button>
<button id="c">Confirm</button>
<button id="p">Prompt</button>

<script>
  document.getElementById("a").addEventListener("click", function () {
    alert("This is an alert.");
  });
  document.getElementById("c").addEventListener("click", function () {
    const ok = confirm("Delete this item?");
    console.log("User chose:", ok);
  });
  document.getElementById("p").addEventListener("click", function () {
    const name = prompt("What's your name?");
    console.log("Name entered:", name);
  });
</script>
  • alert() shows a message with an OK button.
  • confirm() asks OK/Cancel and returns true or false.
  • prompt() asks for text and returns it (or null if cancelled).

These are handy for quick tests, but they block the whole page and look different in every browser. Real websites use custom dialogs built with HTML and CSS.

document.write (avoid)

You may see document.write("Hello") in old tutorials. If it runs after the page has loaded, it erases the whole page. Don't use it.

Debugging with the console

When something doesn't work:

  1. Open the console (F12 → Console).
  2. Look for red error messages. They tell you what went wrong and on which line. Click the file name to jump to the line.
  3. Add console.log() lines to check values step by step.
const items = ["pen", "book"];
console.log("items is:", items);
console.log("first item:", items[0]);
console.log("third item:", items[2]); // undefined: there's no third item

Common mistakes

  • Expecting visitors to see console.log: it's for developers. Use textContent for visitors.
  • **Using innerHTML with user input**, creating a security hole.
  • Regular quotes instead of backticks in template literals: "Hi ${name}" prints the ${name} literally.
  • Leaving lots of console.log calls in finished code. Clean up before publishing.

Exercise

  1. Store your name and age in two variables and print a sentence with a template literal.
  2. Print an array of three friends with console.log and an array of objects with console.table (in your browser console).
  3. Create a page that shows "2 + 2 = 4" inside a paragraph, calculated by JavaScript.
  4. Add a button that uses confirm() and writes "Confirmed" or "Cancelled" into the page.

Summary

  • console.log() prints values for developers; warn, error and table add variety.
  • Template literals (`Hi ${name}`) make messages easy.
  • textContent safely shows text to visitors; use innerHTML only with trusted HTML.
  • alert, confirm and prompt are quick tests, not real UI.

Next, you'll store values in variables with let and const.

items.title: JavaScript Variables (let and const)
items.excerpt: Store values in variables with let and const, learn naming rules, when to use each keyword, and why to avoid the old var.
items.content:
A variable is a named box that stores a value so you can use it later: a user's name, a score, a list of products. Variables are the most basic building block of every program.

Declaring a variable with let

let score = 0;
console.log(score); // 0

score = 10;
console.log(score); // 10

score = score + 5;
console.log(score); // 15
  • let creates (declares) a variable.
  • = assigns a value. In programming, = doesn't mean "equals"; it means "put this value into the box".
  • After declaring a let variable, you can change its value as often as you like.

score = score + 5 reads as: take the current value of score, add 5, and store the result back in score.

Constants with const

const siteName = "VitalStack";
const pi = 3.14159;

console.log(siteName, pi);

// siteName = "Other"; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

const creates a variable that can't be reassigned. Try uncommenting the last line: it causes an error.

Which one to use?

**Use const by default.** Switch to let only when you know the value will change (a counter, a running total, a variable updated in a loop). This makes code easier to understand: when you see const, you know that name always refers to the same value.

const taxRate = 0.18;     // never changes
let total = 0;            // will change

total = total + 100;
total = total + 250;
console.log(`Total with tax: ${total * (1 + taxRate)}`);

const with arrays and objects

const stops you from reassigning the variable, but the contents of an array or object can still change:

const cart = ["pen"];
cart.push("notebook");     // allowed: changing the contents
console.log(cart);         // ["pen", "notebook"]

// cart = ["eraser"];      // error: reassigning the variable

Declaring without a value

let username;
console.log(username); // undefined

username = "rohan_k";
console.log(username);

A variable declared without a value holds undefined. A const must be given a value immediately.

Several variables at once

let x = 1, y = 2, z = 3;
console.log(x + y + z);

This works, but one declaration per line is easier to read.

Naming rules

Names can contain letters, digits, _ and $, but:

  • Can't start with a digit: 1st is invalid, first is fine.
  • Can't contain spaces or hyphens: user-name is invalid.
  • Can't be a reserved word like let, if, function or class.
  • Are case-sensitive: total and Total are different.

Naming conventions

JavaScript developers use camelCase: start lowercase, capitalise each following word.

let firstName = "Meera";
let totalPrice = 1299;
let isLoggedIn = true;
const MAX_UPLOAD_MB = 10; // fixed configuration values are often UPPER_CASE

Choose names that say what the value is: price beats p, userEmails beats arr. Booleans read well with is, has or can: isOpen, hasAccess.

Swapping and updating values

let a = "first";
let b = "second";

let temp = a;
a = b;
b = temp;

console.log(a, b); // "second" "first"

let count = 5;
count += 2;  // same as count = count + 2
count -= 1;  // count = count - 1
count++;     // add 1
console.log(count); // 7

The old var keyword

Before 2015, JavaScript only had var. You'll see it in older code:

var oldStyle = "still works";
console.log(oldStyle);

var has confusing behaviour: it ignores block boundaries like if and for, and can be used before it's declared without an error. let and const fixed these problems. **Don't use var in new code.** You'll understand the details in the Scope lesson.

Common mistakes

  • **Reassigning a const** → TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
  • **Declaring the same let twice** in the same block → SyntaxError: Identifier has already been declared. Declare once, then assign without let.
  • Using a variable before declaring it → ReferenceError.
  • Meaningless names like x1, data2, temp3 in real code.

Exercise

  1. Create const variables for your name and birth year, and a let for the current year. Print your age.
  2. Create let balance = 1000. Subtract a purchase of 250 with -= and add a refund of 50 with +=. Print the result.
  3. Swap the values of two variables using a third one.
  4. Try reassigning a const and read the error message in the output.

Summary

  • Variables store values; = assigns a value.
  • Use const by default, and let when the value must change.
  • Name variables in camelCase with descriptive names.
  • Avoid var in new code.

Next, you'll learn the different types of data a variable can hold.

items.title: JavaScript Data Types
items.excerpt: Strings, numbers, booleans, undefined, null, objects and arrays; checking types with typeof; and how JavaScript converts between types.
items.content:
Every value in JavaScript has a type: text is a string, 42 is a number, true is a boolean. The type decides what you can do with a value: you can multiply numbers but not sentences. Understanding types helps you avoid some of JavaScript's most famous surprises.

The main types

const name = "Asha";             // string
const age = 21;                  // number
const price = 199.5;             // number (no separate decimal type)
const isStudent = true;          // boolean
let nickname;                    // undefined
const middleName = null;         // null
const user = { name: "Asha" };   // object
const skills = ["HTML", "CSS"];  // array (a kind of object)

console.log(typeof name, typeof age, typeof isStudent);

JavaScript has seven primitive types (string, number, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, symbol) plus objects. You'll use the first five and objects every day; bigint and symbol are for special cases.

Strings

Text, written in quotes:

const single = 'Hello';
const double = "Hello";
const template = `Hello, ${single}!`;
console.log(single, double, template);

Single and double quotes work the same. Backticks create template literals with ${ } placeholders. Strings get a whole lesson of their own.

Numbers

console.log(10 + 5);      // 15
console.log(7 / 2);       // 3.5
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);   // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(10 / 0);      // Infinity
console.log("abc" * 2);   // NaN
  • Whole numbers and decimals are the same type.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 because of how computers store decimals. For money, calculate in the smallest unit (paise, cents) or round the result.
  • NaN means "Not a Number": the result of a maths operation that makes no sense.

Booleans

Only two values: true and false. They're the answers to yes/no questions and drive every decision in a program:

const age = 20;
const isAdult = age >= 18;
console.log(isAdult); // true

undefined and null

Both mean "no value", with a small difference:

  • undefined: a value hasn't been set yet. JavaScript uses it automatically: an unassigned variable, a missing object property, a function that returns nothing.
  • null: intentionally empty. You set it yourself to say "there's deliberately nothing here".
let selectedCourse;
console.log(selectedCourse); // undefined: not chosen yet

let winner = null;           // we know there's no winner yet
console.log(winner);

Objects and arrays

Objects group related values under names; arrays hold ordered lists:

const book = { title: "Clean Code", pages: 464, available: true };
const colours = ["red", "green", "blue"];

console.log(book.title);   // "Clean Code"
console.log(colours[0]);   // "red"

Both have full lessons later in this course.

Checking a type with typeof

console.log(typeof "hi");        // "string"
console.log(typeof 3.14);        // "number"
console.log(typeof false);       // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined);   // "undefined"
console.log(typeof {});          // "object"
console.log(typeof []);          // "object" (arrays are objects)
console.log(typeof null);        // "object" (a famous old bug!)
console.log(Array.isArray([]));  // true: the right way to check for arrays

typeof null returning "object" is a mistake from 1995 that can never be fixed without breaking old websites. To check for null, use value === null.

Dynamic typing

A variable can hold any type, and the type can change:

let value = 42;
console.log(typeof value); // "number"
value = "forty-two";
console.log(typeof value); // "string"

This is flexible but can hide bugs. (TypeScript, a popular extension of JavaScript, adds type checking for big projects.)

Type conversion

JavaScript often converts types automatically, sometimes surprisingly:

console.log("5" + 2);   // "52": + with a string joins text
console.log("5" - 2);   // 3: - only works on numbers, so "5" becomes 5
console.log("5" * "2"); // 10
console.log(true + 1);  // 2: true becomes 1

The + rule causes the most bugs: values from form fields are always strings, so "10" + "5" gives "105", not 15.

Convert explicitly to be safe:

const input = "10";
console.log(Number(input) + 5);   // 15
console.log(String(99) + "%");    // "99%"
console.log(parseInt("42px"));    // 42
console.log(parseFloat("3.5kg")); // 3.5
console.log(Number("hello"));     // NaN

Truthy and falsy

In conditions, every value counts as either true or false. These are falsy:

// false, 0, "" (empty string), null, undefined, NaN
console.log(Boolean(0), Boolean(""), Boolean(null));  // false false false
console.log(Boolean("0"), Boolean([]), Boolean("hi")); // true true true

Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false" and empty arrays. You'll use this in if statements: if (username) { ... } runs only when username isn't empty.

Common mistakes

  • Adding form values without converting: "10" + "5" → "105".
  • Checking arrays with typeof instead of Array.isArray().
  • Exact comparisons of decimals like 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 (false).
  • **Confusing null and undefined**; check for both with value == null or explicitly.

Exercise

  1. Create one variable of each main type and print each with its typeof.
  2. Predict the result of "3" + 4 + 5 and 3 + 4 + "5", then check. (Hint: JavaScript works left to right.)
  3. Convert the string "250" to a number and add 50.
  4. Print Boolean() of 0, "0", [], "" and "hello".

Summary

  • Main types: string, number, boolean, undefined, null, object (including arrays).
  • typeof checks a type; use Array.isArray() for arrays and === null for null.
  • + with a string joins text; convert with Number(), String(), parseInt().
  • Falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy.

Next, you'll learn operators for maths, comparison and logic.
items.subject: javascript

items.title: JavaScript Operators
items.excerpt: Arithmetic, assignment, comparison and logical operators, why to use === instead of ==, the ternary operator, and nullish coalescing.
items.content:
Operators are the symbols that do work on values: + adds, > compares, && combines conditions. You've already used a few. This lesson covers all the everyday operators, plus one rule that prevents many bugs: always use ===.

Arithmetic operators

console.log(10 + 3);  // 13  addition
console.log(10 - 3);  // 7   subtraction
console.log(10 * 3);  // 30  multiplication
console.log(10 / 3);  // 3.3333333333333335  division
console.log(10 % 3);  // 1   remainder (modulo)
console.log(2 ** 5);  // 32  exponent (2 to the power 5)

The remainder operator % is more useful than it looks:

const n = 14;
console.log(n % 2 === 0 ? "even" : "odd"); // even
console.log(125 % 60); // 5: 125 seconds is 2 minutes and 5 seconds

Order of operations

Like in maths, *, / and % happen before + and -. Use brackets to make the order clear:

console.log(2 + 3 * 4);   // 14
console.log((2 + 3) * 4); // 20

Increment and decrement

let likes = 10;
likes++;    // 11
likes--;    // 10
console.log(likes);

Assignment operators

let total = 100;
total += 50;  // total = total + 50  → 150
total -= 20;  // total = total - 20  → 130
total *= 2;   // total = total * 2   → 260
total /= 4;   // total = total / 4   → 65
console.log(total);

let greeting = "Hello";
greeting += ", world";
console.log(greeting); // "Hello, world"

Comparison operators

Comparisons produce a boolean, true or false:

console.log(5 > 3);    // true
console.log(5 < 3);    // false
console.log(5 >= 5);   // true
console.log(4 <= 3);   // false
console.log(5 === 5);  // true  equal
console.log(5 !== 3);  // true  not equal

=== vs ==: always use the triple version

console.log(5 == "5");    // true: == converts types before comparing
console.log(5 === "5");   // false: === also checks the type
console.log(0 == "");     // true (!)
console.log(0 === "");    // false
console.log(null == undefined);  // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false

== ("loose equality") converts values to the same type first, which leads to strange results like 0 == "" being true. === ("strict equality") compares value and type, with no surprises.

**Rule: use === and !== everywhere.** If you need to compare a form value with a number, convert it first: Number(input) === 5.

Comparing strings

console.log("apple" < "banana"); // true: alphabetical order
console.log("Zebra" < "apple");  // true: uppercase letters come before lowercase!
console.log("10" < "9");         // true: compared as text, character by character

Strings are compared character by character using their character codes. To compare numbers stored as text, convert them first.

Logical operators

const age = 25;
const hasTicket = true;

console.log(age >= 18 && hasTicket);  // AND: true only if both are true
console.log(age < 12 || age > 60);    // OR: true if at least one is true
console.log(!hasTicket);              // NOT: flips true/false

Short-circuiting

&& and || stop as soon as they know the answer, and return one of the actual values (not always true/false):

const name = "";
console.log(name || "Guest");          // "Guest": || returns the first truthy value

const user = { name: "Asha" };
console.log(user && user.name);        // "Asha": && returns the last value if all are truthy

value || "default" is a classic way to provide a fallback.

Nullish coalescing (??)

|| treats 0 and "" as missing, which is sometimes wrong:

const savedVolume = 0;
console.log(savedVolume || 50);  // 50: wrong, the user chose 0!
console.log(savedVolume ?? 50);  // 0: ?? only falls back on null or undefined

Use ?? when 0, "" or false are valid values.

The ternary operator

A compact if/else that produces a value:

const score = 72;
const result = score >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";
console.log(result); // "Pass"

condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Great for simple choices; use a real if statement for anything longer.

typeof and other operators

You've met typeof. Two more you'll see later: in (does an object have a property?) and instanceof (was an object made from a certain class?).

Common mistakes

  • **Using = in a comparison**: if (x = 5) assigns 5 instead of comparing. Use ===.
  • **Using ==** and getting surprising true results.
  • Comparing numeric strings like "10" < "9".
  • **Using || for defaults** when 0 or "" are valid; use ??.

Exercise

  1. Write code that prints whether 37 is even or odd using %.
  2. Convert 200 minutes into hours and minutes with /, Math.floor() and %.
  3. Given age and hasId, print whether someone can enter a club (18+ and has ID).
  4. Use a ternary to print "Free shipping" if a cart total is 500 or more, otherwise "Add more items".
  5. Compare 0 || 10 with 0 ?? 10 and explain the difference.

Summary

  • Arithmetic: + - * / % **; assignment shortcuts: += -= *= /= ++ --.
  • Comparisons return booleans. **Always use === and !==.**
  • &&, || and ! combine conditions; || and ?? provide defaults.
  • condition ? a : b chooses between two values.

Next, you'll work with text using strings and their methods.
